mood.p: Dinsdag begint nog droog, maar een brede regenzone trekt vanuit het zuidwesten het land binnen en bereikt in de loop van de ochtend het noordwesten, om aan het einde van de middag heel Nederland te bedekken. Het wordt met 16 tot 18 graden een stuk kouder dan de laatste zomerse dagen van afgelopen weekend, er waait een matige zuidwestenwind en de zon laat zich nauwelijks zien. Na de langste droogte in decennia, met de Rijn nog altijd op een historisch laag peil bij Lobith, is de regen ergens welkom voor de watervoorraad, al is de schade aan de scheepvaart en tuinbouw al geleden. De landelijke stemming is gespannen: het kabinet Jetten worstelt met het begrotingsakkoord voor Prinsjesdag over acht dagen, en morgen legt een landelijke OV-staking het treinverkeer plat. Toch zijn er lichtpuntjes. Uit CBS-cijfers blijkt dat jongere generaties over het algemeen vermogender zijn dan hun voorgangers, en de eerste universiteiten zijn deze week weer gevuld met nieuwe studenten die aan het jaar beginnen.

global.h3: US and Iran trade tanker strikes as Hormuz war grinds on
global.summary: Washington and Tehran escalated attacks on oil tankers and warships near the Strait of Hormuz on Monday 7 September, with Iran firing a ballistic missile toward US carriers.
body: The United States targeted three Iranian oil tankers over the weekend while Iran struck back at tankers and fired a ballistic missile toward US aircraft carriers patrolling near the Strait of Hormuz, according to reporting from Al Jazeera. Analysts described Iran's targeting of the carriers as a calculated escalation, noting that the months long conflict is increasingly being fought at sea as both sides try to assert control over the narrow waterway that once carried a fifth of the world's seaborne oil.

Hassan Ghashghavi, a spokesman for the Iranian parliament's national security commission, framed the strikes on US warships as part of what he called an existential war with America, and argued the naval blockade should never have existed. Shipping through Hormuz remains close to a standstill, with tanker traffic reduced to a small fraction of pre war levels, even as diplomats in Muscat say a side deal on a temporary safe corridor is nearly finished.

global.h3: Russian drones hit Kharkiv and Kyiv region on Monday
global.summary: Russian drone strikes injured a resident in Kharkiv and damaged homes and a warehouse near Kyiv on Monday 7 September, as fighting continued alongside stalled peace efforts.
body: A Russian drone struck a civilian facility in Kharkiv's Shevchenkivskyi district on the evening of 7 September, injuring one person, according to updates from Ukrainian outlets. In the Kyiv region, strikes on the same day damaged a private house, a passenger car, a warehouse and an enterprise across the Brovary and Boryspil districts, adding to a steady pattern of nightly drone barrages against Ukrainian population centres.

The strikes came as diplomacy showed little movement. President Volodymyr Zelensky said he expects the war to continue and that Ukraine is counting on American energy and air defence support through the winter, while US special envoy Steve Witkoff said progress had been made toward a new round of trilateral talks. Zelensky also said Ukraine's joint FREYJA anti ballistic missile programme and additional long range strike capability would be discussed at an upcoming meeting of his military staff.

global.h3: Journalists hurt in Gaza and Lebanon as ceasefires fray
global.summary: The Committee to Protect Journalists said reporters in Gaza and Lebanon were injured over the weekend into Monday 7 September, underscoring how fragile the October 2025 ceasefires remain.
body: The Committee to Protect Journalists said it is alarmed by a recent escalation in Israeli strikes on Gaza and Lebanon that injured at least four journalists, three of them on Sunday 6 September. Two of the injured worked for Al Manar TV and were hurt in an Israeli drone strike in southern Lebanon. The group said the attacks show that ceasefires reached last October have done little to protect reporters working in either territory.

Aid officials separately said deliveries into Gaza have fallen to one of their lowest points since the ceasefire took hold, with less food and medical supply entering the strip now than at almost any point since October 2025. Four people were also reported killed in southern Lebanon in Israeli airstrikes that the Israeli military said were a response to Hezbollah drone attacks.

global.h3: North Korea keeps testing missiles as Russia arms flow
global.summary: North Korea fired a barrage of ballistic missiles from Pyongyang in its latest test this year, while Ukrainian intelligence says Pyongyang has begun supplying Russia with newer short range missiles.
body: Japanese and South Korean military authorities detected roughly ten ballistic missiles launched from Pyongyang on 1 September, part of what South Korean assessments count as North Korea's eleventh suspected ballistic missile test of the year following an August 31 launch that flew about 690 kilometres into the Sea of Japan. The pace of testing has accelerated through the summer as Kim Jong Un's government continues to expand its missile programme despite international sanctions.

Ukrainian military intelligence said in late August that Russia has now received its first Hwasong-11C, also known as KN-30, short range ballistic missiles from North Korea, adding to earlier transfers of KN-23 and KN-24 missiles already used against Ukrainian targets. The transfers underline deepening military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow even as North Korea keeps testing new systems closer to home.

global.h3: Sahel violence spreads toward Nigeria and coastal states
global.summary: Armed groups linked to JNIM and Islamic State Sahel province are pushing attacks beyond Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger into Benin, Togo and Nigeria, UN and regional officials warned this month.
body: Militant groups are increasingly using drones, encrypted communications and cryptocurrency to coordinate cross border operations, according to briefings reviewed by regional analysts, as the security crisis that has gripped the Sahel for years now spills into coastal West African states. A UN Security Council briefing said renewed diplomacy is beginning to yield some results even as the terrorist threat continues to grow across the wider region.

The spread of violence has coincided with a widening diplomatic rift between Nigeria and the Sahelian juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, with each new flashpoint hardening rather than softening positions. There have been some positive signs too, including the reopening of the Kamba border crossing between Niger and Nigeria, though aid agencies say only 14 percent of the funding required for this year's humanitarian response across the region has been received so far.

global.h3: AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt vote but falls short of majority
global.summary: Germany's far right Alternative for Germany more than doubled its vote share to win Sunday 6 September's Saxony-Anhalt state election, though it fell just short of an outright majority.
body: The AfD took 43.9 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, a swing of more than 23 points from the 20.8 percent it won at the last election, giving it 39 seats in the state parliament. The result more than doubled the party's previous share and left the long dominant Christian Democrats, who managed just 17.2 percent, a distant second. The Social Democrats came third with 9.3 percent, with the Greens and the Left party close behind.

Despite the historic result, the AfD does not have enough seats to govern alone, and other parties have so far refused to work with it, leaving the shape of the next state government uncertain. Analysts described the outcome as a landmark for the party's eastern German strongholds and a warning sign ahead of further state votes, even as mainstream parties debate whether their long standing refusal to cooperate with the AfD can hold.

global.h3: Iran says Hormuz shipping deal with Oman is days away
global.summary: Tehran said on Monday 7 September that a deal with Oman to manage a temporary safe corridor through the Strait of Hormuz is in its final stages, even as fighting continued at sea.
body: Iranian officials said an agreement with Oman covering a temporary safe shipping route through Hormuz is close to completion after weeks of negotiation, according to Bloomberg. The arrangement is meant to help restore the June 17 ceasefire between Washington and Tehran, resolve the standoff over the strait that once carried a fifth of the world's oil, and open space for wider talks on Iran's nuclear programme.

Washington has pushed back on suggestions that Iran would effectively control traffic through any safe route, insisting that transit should not require Iranian permits, approvals or fees. Hardliners in Tehran have accused the United States of being the real obstacle to a deal, saying the strait will stay closed until their conditions are met, which has left the timeline for any agreement uncertain despite the upbeat statements.

global.h3: Oil hits one month high near $98 on Hormuz fears
global.summary: Brent crude climbed to nearly $98 a barrel on Monday 7 September as renewed Hormuz strikes dimmed hopes the strait would reopen soon.
body: Brent crude touched $97.89 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate topped $92 on 7 September, marking the highest levels since July, as fighting between US and Iranian forces resumed in the strait after roughly a month of relative calm. Both sides struck tankers over the weekend, feeding fears that the flow of oil through the world's most important chokepoint will stay disrupted well into autumn.

Traders were also weighing Iran's claim that a side deal with Oman on a temporary safe corridor is close, which would normally ease prices, but scepticism about whether Washington will accept the terms kept a risk premium baked into the market. The US Energy Information Administration has already lifted its price outlook to reflect what it calls a reshaped forecast driven by the ongoing Hormuz crisis.

global.h3: Trump asks Supreme Court to block mailed ballots in transit
global.summary: President Trump asked the Supreme Court on Sunday 6 September to let the Postal Service refuse to deliver or return ballots already in the mail, his third such bid in six weeks.
body: Trump's request would let the US Postal Service withhold delivery or return of ballots that are already in transit, an escalation of a fight over mail voting rules that has already reached the high court twice in recent weeks. A federal judge had blocked the underlying Postal Service rule, ruling that no state could comply in time since it would require every state to redesign ballot envelopes, secure approval for the new design and upload each voter's name and address to a federal portal.

The petition landed as Trump spent the Labor Day holiday in Bedminster, New Jersey, with plans to return to Washington to mark the 25th anniversary of September 11 later in the week. Separately in Washington, a bipartisan push to raise the payroll tax gained traction as a way to avoid deep cuts to retirement benefits, even drawing interest from some Republicans normally opposed to any tax increase.

global.h3: Congress presses White House on Venezuela war powers
global.summary: Lawmakers continued to question the legal basis for US military operations tied to Venezuela on Monday 7 September, months after the January capture of Nicolas Maduro.
body: Eight months after US forces captured former Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in a January raid, congressional scrutiny of the broader military campaign has intensified. The Senate recently voted down a bipartisan war powers resolution that would have required congressional authorisation before further US military action in or against Venezuela, a defeat for lawmakers who argue the campaign has operated with insufficient oversight.

Human rights groups have continued to question the legality of a string of earlier strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats that preceded the Maduro operation, arguing the campaign set a troubling precedent for unilateral use of force in the region. Defense officials have defended the operations as necessary counter narcotics and security measures.

global.h3: France's revolving door government still hunting a budget
global.summary: France entered the week with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu still trying to stabilise a governing majority as the country's fourth government in a year works toward a budget deal.
body: Lecornu, who was appointed in September 2025, briefly resigned in October and was then reappointed within days, remains the fourth prime minister to hold the post in roughly a year. His predecessor Francois Bayrou was ousted after failing to build a stable majority following a confidence vote tied to his austerity budget, continuing a pattern of parliamentary fragmentation that has dogged French politics since the 2024 snap elections.

With the next presidential contest not scheduled until April or May 2027, an early legislative election looks unlikely, leaving Lecornu to govern with a fragile coalition through further budget negotiations. Analysts note the instability has made it harder for Paris to commit to shared European positions on everything from defence spending to the bloc's response to the Hormuz crisis.

global.h3: Small boats protests flare at Portsmouth and Dover
global.summary: Demonstrations over Channel crossings broke out at Portsmouth and the Port of Dover as UK lawmakers returned to Westminster on Monday 7 September for a new sitting week.
body: A protest in Portsmouth over small boat arrivals prompted the local police and crime commissioner to call the unrest a wake up call for the government, while separate demonstrations were also reported at the Port of Dover. The protests added pressure on ministers as parliament resumed business, with the Commons taking up housing, communities and local government questions followed by remaining stages of the Health Bill.

In the House of Lords, members debated draft legislation to nationalise the rail network through the creation of Great British Railways, a flagship plan from the government to bring train operations back under public control. Immigration policy and small boat crossings remain among the most politically charged issues facing the government heading into the autumn parliamentary session.

global.h3: Sudan's war leaves 33.7 million needing aid in 2026
global.summary: Nearly three years of conflict in Sudan has pushed 33.7 million people, half of them children, into need of humanitarian assistance, aid agencies said in updates current through early September.
body: Sudan's civil war has driven mass displacement, food insecurity and disease outbreaks that have collapsed essential services across the country, according to the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan tracked on ReliefWeb. Eastern Africa as a whole is now one of the world's most severe humanitarian hotspots, with 48.5 million people across the region in need this year, and aid officials say the parallel Middle East conflict is disrupting supply routes and pushing up fuel and food costs.

A first standard allocation of 40 million dollars from the Sudan Humanitarian Fund is meant to plug some of the most critical gaps, but agencies say funding remains far short of what is needed. In South Sudan, conflict around Nasir is separately sustaining an emergency level food crisis and a risk of famine that has persisted from April through September.

global.h3: Famine confirmed in El Fasher as siege toll mounts
global.summary: Food security monitors have confirmed famine conditions in Sudan's El Fasher and Kadugli, with rights groups saying tens of thousands fled North Darfur after the city's fall.
body: The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification system has confirmed famine in El Fasher and Kadugli, with twenty other areas of Sudan at risk of crossing the same threshold. Amnesty International has said the Rapid Support Forces committed ethnic cleansing during its siege of El Fasher, which ran from May 2024 until the city's fall in October 2025, restricting food and aid while shelling the city almost daily and forcing residents to eat ambaz, a peanut byproduct normally fed to animals.

Roughly 61.7 percent of Sudan's population, or 28.9 million people, are now facing acute food shortages nationwide. Aid workers warn that El Obeid, now under siege by the Rapid Support Forces, could become the next city to face conditions similar to those that produced famine in El Fasher.

global.h3: 2026 on track to be second warmest year on record
global.summary: Carbon Brief's tracking shows 2026 is likely to rank as the second or third warmest year on record globally, with ocean surface temperatures still running at record levels into September.
body: Carbon Brief's state of the climate analysis puts 2026 roughly tied with 2023 and 2025 for the warmest years measured, with a strong El Nino expected to develop further later in the year and push temperatures higher still. Daily global sea surface temperatures hit 20.86 degrees Celsius in June, breaking the previous record of 20.83 degrees set on the same date in 2023 and 2024, and ocean heat has stayed at record levels every day since.

Scientists tracking the pattern say the persistence of record ocean warmth, layered on top of a developing El Nino, makes further extreme heat events more likely into the autumn. Europe and the United States have already recorded shocking extreme heat this year that has surprised climate scientists monitoring long term trends.

global.h3: El Obeid siege raises fears of a second Sudan famine
global.summary: Aid monitors warned this month that El Obeid, now surrounded by Rapid Support Forces fighters, could face a famine similar to the one confirmed in El Fasher.
body: Analysts tracking the siege said the pattern around El Obeid closely mirrors the months long blockade that preceded confirmed famine conditions in El Fasher and Kadugli, with humanitarian access into the city sharply restricted. Aid groups say the risk illustrates how quickly localised sieges in Sudan's civil war can tip into full blown famine once food and medical supplies are cut off for an extended period.

The warning comes as international donors continue to struggle to fund Sudan's response plan, with the country's overall humanitarian caseload now standing at 33.7 million people in need. Aid officials say the parallel Middle East conflict has made the funding and logistics picture even harder, diverting attention and resources away from a crisis that is already one of the world's largest.

netherlands.h3: Jetten cabinet races to finish budget before Prinsjesdag
netherlands.summary: With Prinsjesdag just over a week away on 15 September, the Jetten minority cabinet was still trying on Monday 7 September to secure enough opposition support to pass its budget.
body: Finance minister Eelco Heinen must have a finished budget ready for his traditional black briefcase by Prinsjesdag, but as of Monday the cabinet still lacked firm commitments from enough opposition parties in both the Second and First Chamber. Because the coalition governs without a majority, it needs broad support from left and right leaning opposition parties to get the Miljoenennota through parliament, and initial signals were not encouraging.

Leaked details suggest the government has largely abandoned planned cuts to social security and will delay a planned increase in the health insurance deductible by a year, while setting aside 1.5 billion euros to help restore household purchasing power. GroenLinks-PvdA leader Jesse Klaver said he had heard nothing further from prime minister Rob Jetten since their last conversation and worried that difficult choices were being postponed rather than made.

netherlands.h3: Nationwide transport strike set to halt trains on Wednesday
netherlands.summary: Unions confirmed a 24 hour strike will hit NS, ProRail, DB Cargo and city transit on Wednesday 9 September over planned cuts to unemployment and disability benefits.
body: FNV members at NS, ProRail, DB Cargo, regional bus operators and city transit companies including GVB, RET and HTM will down tools for a full day on Wednesday, with NS train staff walking out from 02:00 that morning until 02:00 on Thursday. ProRail confirmed to trade outlet SpoorPro that essentially no trains will run nationwide, with only the Airport Sprinter between Amsterdam Central, Schiphol and Hoofddorp continuing to operate.

The union says the strike is meant to send an unmistakable signal to The Hague that plans to further tighten unemployment and disability insurance are unacceptable and must be dropped from the budget entirely. FNV confirmed on Monday that despite ongoing budget talks, the cuts were not yet off the table and the strike would go ahead as planned.

netherlands.h3: Rutte faces corona commission for a second and final time
netherlands.summary: Former prime minister Mark Rutte answered questions from the parliamentary Covid inquiry commission on Monday 7 September in what was billed as its last week of public hearings.
body: Rutte appeared before the commission from 10:00 on Monday morning to account for his cabinet's handling of the pandemic, in what was described as his second and final hearing before the panel. The session fell in the commission's closing week of public testimony, after which it is expected to move toward drafting its final conclusions on the government's coronavirus response.

Commentators noted the commission still had many open questions for Rutte specifically around what has been called the method Rutte, his hands on approach to steering cabinet decisions during the pandemic, and whether he remained genuinely open to internal criticism of the government's Covid strategy at the time.

netherlands.h3: Housing shortfall grows to 410,000 homes nationwide
netherlands.summary: The Netherlands is now about 410,000 homes short of what its population needs, CBS figures confirmed this week, up from 400,000 a year earlier.
body: The shortage now represents 4.8 percent of the national housing stock, and only 69,189 new homes were completed in 2025, well below the government's annual target of 100,000. Officials point to a mix of causes including nitrogen emission rules that delay building permits, high construction material costs, municipal planning processes that can take eight to twelve years from start to finish, and an electricity grid too congested to easily support new developments.

House prices continue to climb even as supply grows slightly, with Rabobank's housing market quarterly showing no clear signs of cooling. The price index for existing owner occupied homes rose 8.57 percent year on year in 2025 before easing to a still brisk 4.98 percent in March 2026, leaving first time buyers, particularly younger Gen Z buyers, struggling to enter the market.

netherlands.h3: CBS: younger generations wealthier than their parents were
netherlands.summary: New CBS data published Monday 7 September found that, contrary to popular perception, younger generations in the Netherlands are generally wealthier at the same age than the generations before them.
body: Statistics Netherlands compared wealth accumulation across generations at equivalent ages and found today's younger adults hold more assets on average than their predecessors did, even as concerns about housing affordability and stagnant purchasing power dominate political debate. The finding complicates the common narrative that younger Dutch households are falling behind financially compared with earlier generations.

Researchers cautioned that averages can mask large disparities, since homeownership, inheritance and regional differences all shape individual wealth trajectories very differently. The report lands just as the housing shortage and rental crisis remain central themes in the run up to Prinsjesdag budget negotiations.

netherlands.h3: Record low Rhine keeps freshwater and shipping under strain
netherlands.summary: Weeks after the Rhine hit its lowest recorded level at the Dutch border, the drought's economic toll on shipping and horticulture is still being tallied heading into autumn.
body: The Rhine's discharge at Lobith fell below 615 cubic metres per second in mid August, breaking the previous record low set during the 2022 drought, and the river's level dropped to 6.47 metres above NAP. The Netherlands has since moved back down from a level two to a level one water shortage classification after weeks of rain, but officials say the reduced river volume will continue to be felt for months.

The government estimates damage to businesses, from inland shipping operators to greenhouse horticulture, at tens to hundreds of millions of euros, with restrictions on lock operations introduced in several regions to conserve freshwater. The delta commissioner has separately warned that the Netherlands needs to roughly double its water infrastructure spending, a recommendation expected to feature in the full 2027 Delta Programme due on Prinsjesdag.

netherlands.h3: Delta commissioner urges doubling of water spending
netherlands.summary: The Netherlands must roughly double what it spends on water infrastructure, the country's delta commissioner warned this week ahead of the full 2027 Delta Programme due on Prinsjesdag.
body: The warning follows a summer in which the Rhine hit its lowest recorded water level at the Dutch border and the government was forced to formally declare a national water shortage. The commissioner argues that current investment levels are not enough to protect the country against a future of more frequent droughts and more extreme rainfall, both linked to climate change.

The full revised Delta Programme strategy will be published alongside the national budget on 15 September, giving parliament its first detailed look at how much extra funding the government is prepared to commit. Water boards and provinces have separately pressed The Hague for clarity on financing, warning that further delays could leave both freshwater supply and flood defences increasingly exposed.

netherlands.h3: PISA 2025 results land Tuesday amid reading concerns
netherlands.summary: The new PISA 2025 scores were due for release on Tuesday 8 September, with Dutch education watchers bracing for another weak result after a sharp decline in reading ability.
body: In the last PISA round, Dutch secondary students scored 459 points in reading, well below both the EU average of 480 and the OECD average of 476, placing the Netherlands second lowest in Europe after Greece. Roughly a third of Dutch students are now considered insufficiently literate, and the decline has accelerated markedly since the 2018 round, outpacing the average drop seen across other EU14 countries.

Education researchers have linked the slide to reduced reading for pleasure among teenagers and changes in how Dutch language exams are structured, and the new figures released this week were expected to show whether recent literacy campaigns have made any dent in the trend. The results carry political weight too, since school quality has become a recurring theme in budget debates ahead of Prinsjesdag.

netherlands.h3: Fortuna Sittard beats promoted ADO Den Haag on the road
netherlands.summary: Fortuna Sittard continued its strong start to the Eredivisie season with an away win over newly promoted ADO Den Haag on Sunday 6 September.
body: Fortuna Sittard travelled to the WerkTalent Stadion sitting sixth in the table with seven points from four matches, while hosts ADO Den Haag were second from bottom with just a single point from their opening four games back in the top flight after a five year absence. It was the two clubs' first Eredivisie meeting since ADO's relegation five seasons ago.

The result extended Fortuna's positive form under coach Robin Peters and left ADO still searching for their first win since returning to the Eredivisie. The Limburg club's start has drawn attention as one of the division's early surprises, while ADO faces mounting pressure to secure results before the international break.

netherlands.h3: Universities open their doors for the new academic year
netherlands.summary: Dutch universities in Amsterdam, Leiden, Utrecht and elsewhere welcomed students back for the first semester in the first week of September.
body: The start of the academic year brought the usual wave of introduction events, housing scrambles and orientation activities across university towns, with IamExpat noting that international students in particular continue to face a tight and sometimes scam prone rental market as they search for rooms near campus.

The timing coincides with mounting attention on the housing shortage more broadly, as students compete with other groups for a limited supply of affordable rooms in university cities. Universities have repeated calls for more purpose built student housing as enrolment, including from international students, continues to grow year over year.

netherlands.h3: Waste Free Week kicks off with local food saving drives
netherlands.summary: The national Waste Free Week began this week, with entrepreneurs in Panningen among those organising local efforts to cut daily food waste.
body: Local businesses in Panningen partnered up during the campaign week to redistribute surplus food that would otherwise be thrown away, part of a broader national push highlighted by NOS to reduce the large quantities of edible food Dutch households and retailers discard every day.

Campaigners used the week to press supermarkets and restaurants to donate more unsold food to charities and food banks, framing the effort as both an environmental and a cost of living measure at a time when household budgets are under pressure from high grocery prices.

netherlands.h3: Last taste of summer gives way to autumn rain
netherlands.summary: Monday 7 September brought the season's final warm spell, with highs up to 29 degrees in Limburg, before a wet and much cooler Tuesday moved in.
body: Temperatures ranged from a milder 24 degrees on the coast up to 29 degrees in Limburg and along the eastern border on Monday, giving much of the country one last summery day before autumn weather arrived. Forecasters had flagged the shift for days, describing Monday as the last chance to enjoy shorts and terraces before a broad frontal system moved in.

By Tuesday 8 September, a low pressure system over Scotland pushed a wide band of rain across the country, dropping daytime highs to 16 to 18 degrees with a fresh southwesterly wind and almost no sunshine. The cooler, wetter pattern is expected to persist into midweek, arriving just as the country braces for Wednesday's nationwide transport strike.
